text: Most quantities depend on more than one thing. The error of a neural network depends on every one of its weights at once, so we need a way to ask how the error changes when we nudge just one of them. That is exactly what a partial derivative measures.

Picture a function of two inputs as a hilly landscape. The two inputs say where you are standing, and the output is the height of the ground beneath your feet. You can walk east, or north, or in any direction in between, and how steep the walk feels depends on which way you face.

A partial derivative makes the question simple again by freezing every input but one. Hold y fixed, and you are walking along a single east to west slice through the hill, which is an ordinary curve with an ordinary slope. That slope is the partial derivative with respect to x, written with a curly d to remind you that the other inputs are being held still.

Computing it uses nothing new: treat every other variable as a constant and differentiate as usual. For f equal to x squared plus two y squared, the partial derivative with respect to x is two x, because the y term does not change while only x moves. In the same way, the partial derivative with respect to y is four y.

Now take the other slice, running north to south with x frozen, and read off the second partial. At any point, the two partials together give the slope of the ground facing east and the slope facing north, and for a smooth surface those two numbers are enough to work out the slope facing any direction at all.

You can also measure a partial derivative numerically, with the same trick as before: nudge one input by a tiny amount, leave the others alone, and divide the change in the output by the size of the nudge. Doing this for each input in turn is slow when there are millions of inputs, which is why networks use backpropagation instead, but it remains the standard way to check that backpropagation is correct.

For a language model, the loss is a single number that depends on billions of weights, and every training step needs the partial derivative of that loss with respect to each one of them. Next, we gather all those partial derivatives into a single arrow, the gradient, and see that it points uphill.
